title: One in five refineries at closure risk as global oil demand peaks in 2032
gist: Wood Mackenzie forecasts global refined product demand rising from 105 mb/d to a 2032 peak of 108 mb/d before structural decline, leaving about 20% of global refining capacity on a 'downward escalator' toward closure. Exposure is sharply uneven across five refinery archetypes: large complex and chemical-integrated sites can adapt, while European coastal crackers and small low-complexity NOC plants are most vulnerable; current elevated margins from the Middle East conflict and Russian refinery damage are seen as temporary.

themes.theme: Oil demand peak and closure risk

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts global refined product demand will rise from 105 million barrels per day in 2025 to a peak of 108 mb/d in 2032, then enter structural decline.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sets a 2032 horizon for terminal-demand risk across downstream oil assets.

insights.claim: Roughly 20% of the world's existing refining capacity, out of more than 700 refineries, sits on a 'downward escalator' of falling or negative operating net cash margins and rising closure risk.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Capacity rationalization could support margins for surviving refiners.

insights.claim: With 2040 only three to four refinery turnaround cycles away, the window for major refinery investment decisions is closing even though the demand peak is in 2032.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Capex decisions in the next few years lock in which refiners survive.

insights.claim: Alan Gelder of Wood Mackenzie says the industry for the first time faces sustained decline in end-market demand rather than a temporary supply disruption, and that lacking a credible adaptation plan is effectively a decision to decline.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Management inaction at weaker refiners should be treated as a negative signal.
insights.quote: For those without structural advantages, the absence of a credible adaptation plan is not a deferral. It is a decision.
insights.locator: The sector has navigated structural change

insights.claim: India will account for 40% of global refining capacity additions to 2030, driven by domestic demand growth and energy self-reliance policy, even though it adds capacity into a global market in structural decline.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: New Indian capacity adds competitive pressure on export-dependent refiners elsewhere.

insights.claim: Gasoline faces the sharpest demand pressure from EV adoption, while diesel, gasoil and jet fuel are more resilient because heavy road transport and aviation lack clear decarbonisation pathways.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gasoline-heavy refinery yields are most exposed; middle-distillate cracks better supported.
insights.locator: The demand decline is not uniform

insights.claim: LPG and naphtha benefit from petrochemical feedstock demand, and specialty products such as lubricants, bitumen and waxes are largely insulated because bio-based alternatives do not yet exist at scale.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Specialty and petchem-feedstock-oriented assets have defensive demand profiles.
insights.locator: The demand decline is not uniform

insights.claim: Current elevated refining margins, driven by the Middle East conflict and damage to Russian refineries, will revert to more modest levels when the conflict ends, since margins depend on crack spreads rather than oil prices and long-run benchmark margins are slim.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Current refiner earnings are cyclically inflated; valuations should not extrapolate them.

insights.claim: Refining generates lower returns on capital than upstream oil operations, making adaptation investment harder to fund precisely when it is most needed.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet strength becomes a key differentiator among refiners.

insights.claim: Large-scale, high-complexity refineries such as major US Gulf Coast assets, modern Middle East export facilities and Nigeria's Dangote refinery, together with complex chemical-integrated sites common in China, have the broadest adaptation options and are best placed to become integrated energy parks.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Scale and complexity identify likely long-term winners in refining.

insights.claim: Coastal cracking refineries, the most common OECD configuration, face direct international competition and narrower options, with European assets under the most acute regional pressure, while small low-complexity refineries, many NOC-owned in developing countries, survive only through subsidies.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: European coastal refiners are the most likely closure candidates.
insights.locator: Coastal cracking refineries, the most common

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie scores refinery complexity on a 1-to-25 scale, and higher scores generally correlate with higher net cash margins.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Complexity score is a usable screen for refinery asset quality.

insights.claim: Petrochemical integration, redirecting LPG and naphtha into olefins, aromatics and polymers, is the main route for large complex sites and is led by state-backed Asian and Middle Eastern operators, while bio and circular conversion to renewable diesel and SAF suits EU coastal refineries.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: State capital gives Asian and Gulf refiners an edge in petchem integration.
insights.locator: Many pathways exist, but not all

insights.claim: For mid-tier refineries the realistic options are capacity consolidation, a pivot to specialty products, full value-chain integration, or diversification into power, LNG and ammonia, while CCS is relevant mainly to European and OECD operators.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Expect consolidation M&A and repurposing among mid-tier refiners.
insights.locator: Many pathways exist, but not all

insights.claim: Chris Barry of Wood Mackenzie warns of a mismatch between refiners' adaptation ambitions and balance sheet capacity, arguing structurally weaker sites should consolidate around local market strength or move into specialty products rather than chase petrochemical or renewable fuels integration.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Ambitious transition capex at weak refiners may destroy value.
insights.quote: The risk is a mismatch between ambition and balance sheet capacity.
insights.locator: The capital required for the most

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects a bifurcated refining sector of world-class integrated energy and molecule parks at one end and terminal conversion, repurposing or closure at the other, with specialists surviving on local feedstock, regulatory or state-support advantages.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Investors should assess each refinery's archetype, location and ownership rather than the sector as a whole.
insights.quote: the question is not whether a refinery will face pressure, but whether its archetype, location and ownership structure give it the tools to adapt

insights.claim: Sustainable aviation fuels can deliver up to an 80% emissions reduction versus conventional jet fuel.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Supports SAF as a decarbonisation lever for refinery conversions.
